summary: Presents an object-oriented information model for representing Quality of Service (QoS) network management policies. It builds on the IETF Policy Core Information Model and covers QoS enforcement for differentiated and integrated services. As an information model, it is independent of any particular storage or protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Rules like which messages get to go first need to be written in a common way. This is a blueprint for describing such priority rules so different tools can understand them.

subtitle: A vendor-neutral way to write down QoS rules, such as who gets bandwidth first, before any device is configured.

tldr.problem: Administrators think of QoS in terms of business goals, but devices from different vendors are configured in very different ways, so a policy written for one box does not carry over to another.
tldr.mechanism: The QoS Policy Information Model (QPIM) extends the IETF Policy Core Information Model with classes for QoS actions, traffic profiles and RSVP variables, so rules of the form condition-then-action can be written once and mapped to devices by policy servers.
tldr.outcome: QPIM standardizes how QoS policy is represented for differentiated and integrated services. It is only a model, independent of any storage mechanism or access protocol.

sections.title: What QPIM Is
sections.content:
The QoS Policy Information Model (QPIM) is a framework of classes and relationships for specifying policies that administer, manage and control access to network QoS resources. It is based on the Policy Core Information Model (RFC 3060) and its extensions (RFC 3460), and it targets QoS enforcement for differentiated and integrated services.

It is an information model, so it is independent of any particular data storage mechanism and access protocol. Directory schemata, relational database schemata and SNMP MIBs can all be designed from the one model. QPIM is aimed at large-scale policy domains and at helping human administrators define policy, not at configuring individual network elements.

The administrator works from three inputs: network topology, the QoS methodology (for example Differentiated Services) and business rules. Topology and business rules are outside the scope of QPIM.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a shared way of writing down the rules for who goes first on a network, so that every tool reads the rules the same way.

sections.title: Design Goals
sections.content:
QPIM is policy-definition oriented. A rule has a condition clause and an action clause: if the condition is true, the QoS actions can be executed. The RFC's example is that web traffic should get at least 50% of the bandwidth, written as If protocol == HTTP then minimum BW = 50%. QPIM deliberately did not subclass the PolicyRule class, because that would make it harder to combine actions and conditions from different functional domains in one rule.

The other goals follow from that:

  • Goal-oriented: the writer states a minimal desired behavior and policy servers (PDPs) fill in device details such as queue lengths.
  • Device and vendor independent: roles map a policy to many devices, so a small set of policies can cover a large heterogeneous network.
  • Reusable: variables, values, actions, traffic profiles, groups and rules can be shared. Changing a central value such as a finance subnet updates every rule that refers to it.
  • Enforceable and interoperable: a PDP must be able to map the policy to PEP configurations, but the same policy need not yield the same configuration on every device.
sections.plainLanguage: You say what you want, like 'video gets priority', and each device works out how to do it, the way a boss gives a goal and each worker picks the tools.

sections.title: Rule Hierarchy
sections.content:
Rules and groups can be nested, using the PolicySetComponent aggregation from RFC 3460. In QPIM the nesting also carries meaning: bandwidth actions in a sub-rule divide up the bandwidth given to the parent rule's traffic class, and drop threshold actions in a sub-rule act on the parent rule's queue.

The RFC's example guarantees 30% of the interface to UDP and 40% to TCP. Sub-rules then give TFTP 10% and NFS 40% of the UDP share, and HTTP 20% and FTP 30% of the TCP share. A flat version of the same rules gives 3%, 12%, 8% and 12% of the whole interface. The two are not identical: a UDP flow that is neither TFTP nor NFS is guaranteed 30% in the hierarchical form but only 15% in the flat form. The RFC concludes that rules with hierarchy should be enforced with hierarchical schedulers.

Hierarchy for bandwidth and for drop thresholds should not be mixed in the same sub-rules. If both refinements are needed, the threshold rules and the bandwidth rules should each go in their own group, and both groups are aggregated under the parent rule.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like cutting a cake into big slices and then cutting one slice again. A small piece is a share of its slice, not of the whole cake.

sections.title: Class and Association Hierarchies
sections.content:
QPIM's classes are rooted in the classes of RFC 3060 and RFC 3460 and add their own. The action classes fall under PolicyAction. The traffic profile classes derive from the abstract QoSPolicyTrfcProf. The RSVP variable classes derive from QoSPolicyRSVPVariable, and two value classes, QoSPolicyDNValue and QoSPolicyAttributeValue, extend PolicyValue.

Associations derive from the Dependency association. They link an admission action to its traffic profile, and a policing action to the actions for conforming, exceeding and violating traffic. The figures in the RFC are not complete: designers must also use classes such as SimplePolicyCondition from the core documents.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a family tree for the building blocks. Each new block is a child of an older one and inherits what it can do.

sections.title: QoS Actions
sections.content:
QoS actions are the network behaviors applied to traffic selected by conditions. The RFC groups them in four sets: QoSPolicyRSVPSimpleAction, admission actions, per-hop behavior (PHB) actions and the unconditional discard action QoSPolicyDiscardAction. Some actions, such as the DSCP, IP precedence and layer-2 CoS markers, are modeled with SimplePolicyAction plus variables and values.

RSVP actions

Following COPS usage for RSVP (RFC 2749), one action class makes admit-or-reject decisions and another controls the other two decision types. qpRSVPActionType is REPLACE, STATELESS or REPLACEANDSTATELESS. It can, for example, set a preemption priority or control the DSCP mapping through the DCLASS variable.

Admission, policing and shaping

An admission action is tied to a traffic profile and has a scope: 0 meters each flow on its own, 1 meters all matching flows as one aggregate. The RFC's example polices each HTTP flow to 64kb/s and all HTTP together to 512Kb/s, using two police actions with the rule's ExecutionStrategy set to Do All. A police action is paired with conform, exceed and violate actions. A shaper delays packets to fit a profile, and the only required association is the traffic profile.

Per-hop behavior

QoSPolicyBandwidthAction sets minimum and maximum bandwidth, forwarding priority, maximum delay and jitter in milliseconds, and fairness. QoSPolicyCongestionControlAction sets queue size, drop method (tail-drop, head-drop or random-drop) and drop thresholds. The RFC's AF1 example uses thresholds of 6 and 16 packets for AF11, 4 and 13 for AF12, and 2 and 10 for AF13.
sections.plainLanguage: An action is what the network does with a message: let it through, slow it down, give it a priority sticker, or throw it away.

sections.title: Traffic Profiles
sections.content:
A traffic profile is what a meter compares traffic against. The provisioning profile, QoSPolicyTokenBucketTrfcProf, has a rate in kbits/sec, a normal burst in bytes and an excess burst in bytes. Traffic under the rate and within the normal burst is conforming. Traffic above the normal burst but within the excess burst is exceeding, and traffic beyond the excess burst is violating. A zero excess burst means none is allowed.

The RSVP profile, QoSPolicyIntServTrfcProf, has seven properties: token rate r, peak rate p, bucket size b, minimum policed unit m, maximum packet size M, reserve rate R and slack term s. The first five describe a TSPEC or a Controlled-Load FLOWSPEC, and R and s are for a Guaranteed Service FLOWSPEC. An RSVP message is accepted only if its TSPEC or FLOWSPEC is smaller than or equal to the profile, and the RFC defines how to add TSPECs so a whole class can be compared.
sections.plainLanguage: A traffic profile is a speed limit with some give. Go under it and you are fine, go a bit over and you are warned, go far over and you are stopped.

sections.title: RSVP Variables and Values
sections.content:
The RFC defines 17 pre-defined RSVP variable classes so policy servers and tools from different vendors can use the same terms in conditions and actions. They cover the source and destination addresses (IPv4 and IPv6) and ports of a signaled flow, the IP protocol and version, the DCLASS DSCP value, the reservation style, the requested Integrated Service type, the RSVP message type, the two preemption priorities, the user, the application and the authentication method. All extend QoSPolicyRSVPVariable.

Two value classes support them. QoSPolicyDNValue holds Distinguished Names, including wildcards, and QoSPolicyAttributeValue names which property of a multi-attribute object to match. For instance, a condition can match the RSVP user's last name by pairing a user variable with an attribute name and a value list.
sections.plainLanguage: Variables are the labels on a message that a rule can look at, such as who sent it, where it is going and which program made it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The Policy Core Information Model describes the general security considerations for the core policy model. This document states that its extensions do not introduce any additional security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: The model adds no new safety worries beyond those of the model it builds on.
